quests.instruction: Which parts of you should be brushed for two minutes, morning and night?
quests.hint: They are hard and white, with a shiny coating called enamel.
quests.explanation: Brushing for two minutes, morning and night, removes food and sticky germs that can cause cavities.
quests.funFact: Toothpaste has fluoride, a mineral that helps make tooth enamel stronger.

quests.instruction: Germs and food bits can coat which part inside your mouth, so a gentle brush there helps keep your breath fresh?
quests.hint: It is soft and pink, and it is bumpy on top.
quests.explanation: A thin coating can build up on the bumpy surface of the tongue, which is why brushing it gently can help.
quests.funFact: Most bad breath starts in the mouth.

quests.instruction: Which soft, pink parts hold your teeth in place and need gentle brushing, too?
quests.hint: Healthy ones are pink and do not bleed when you brush.
quests.explanation: Gums wrap around the base of each tooth. Brushing gently along them keeps them healthy.
quests.funFact: More than half of each tooth is hidden below the gums.

quests.instruction: Before you eat, which parts of your body should you scrub with soap and water for about 20 seconds?
quests.hint: They touch doorknobs, toys, and food.
quests.explanation: Soap lifts germs off your skin, and water rinses them away. Scrubbing for about 20 seconds does the job.
quests.funFact: Singing the happy birthday song twice takes about 20 seconds.

quests.instruction: Which parts should you keep short and clean, because dirt and germs can hide underneath them?
quests.hint: A nailbrush can help clean under them.
quests.explanation: Dirt collects under the edges of fingernails, so scrub there when you wash your hands.
quests.funFact: Biting your nails can carry germs straight to your mouth.

quests.instruction: You feel a sneeze coming and have no tissue. Into which part of your arm should you sneeze to keep germs off your hands?
quests.hint: It is the joint you can bend up to cover your nose and mouth.
quests.explanation: Sneezing into the bent elbow catches the droplets and keeps them off the things your hands touch.
quests.funFact: A sneeze can spray tiny droplets a few meters.

quests.instruction: Which part do you wash gently with a soft cloth and water, taking care not to get soap in your eyes?
quests.hint: It holds your eyes, nose, and mouth.
quests.explanation: Washing your face removes dirt and extra oil from the skin.
quests.funFact: The skin on your face is thinner than the skin on your palms or the soles of your feet.

quests.instruction: After a bath, which parts need extra drying in the spaces between them, so the skin stays healthy?
quests.hint: They are the five small parts at the end of each foot.
quests.explanation: Warm, damp places between the toes can grow an itchy fungus, so dry them well.
quests.funFact: Athlete's foot got its name because it spreads in damp places like locker rooms, where athletes walk barefoot.

quests.instruction: Tiny insects called lice can live on which part of the head, so it is wise not to share combs and hats?
quests.hint: It grows from your scalp.
quests.explanation: Lice crawl from one head of hair to another, so sharing combs, hats, and hair ties can pass them along.
quests.funFact: Lice cannot jump or fly. They only crawl.

quests.instruction: Which part do you blow gently, one side at a time, into a tissue when it is stuffy?
quests.hint: Sniffling is a sign that it needs clearing.
quests.explanation: Gentle blowing clears mucus. Blowing too hard can push mucus toward your ears and cause pressure.
quests.funFact: Throw the tissue away and wash your hands afterward, because mucus can carry germs.

quests.instruction: You scrape your knee on the sidewalk. Which part of your body got broken, and should be rinsed with clean water?
quests.hint: It is the layer that covers your whole body.
quests.explanation: A scrape breaks the skin, so rinsing helps wash out dirt before it can cause an infection.
quests.funFact: A scab is a natural bandage that protects the skin underneath while it heals.

quests.instruction: Rubbing which parts of your body with dirty hands can spread germs into them?
quests.hint: Tears help keep them clean.
quests.explanation: Germs on your hands can slip into your eyes when you rub them. Wash your hands first, and tell a grown-up if your eyes feel sore.
quests.funFact: Tears contain a substance that helps fight germs.

quests.instruction: New shoes that rub can cause a blister on the back of which part of your foot?
quests.hint: It is the rounded back of your foot.
quests.explanation: A heel can get rubbed again and again inside a stiff or loose shoe, which can cause a blister.
quests.funFact: A blister is filled with clear fluid that cushions the damaged skin underneath.

quests.instruction: Clean, dry socks help keep which parts of your body comfortable and healthy?
quests.hint: Shoes go over them.
quests.explanation: Socks soak up sweat and cushion your feet inside your shoes.
quests.funFact: Cotton and wool socks soak up moisture better than many slick materials.

quests.instruction: Sunscreen is a lotion you put on bare areas to protect which part of your body from sunburn?
quests.hint: It can turn red and sore if it stays too long in strong sun.
quests.explanation: Sunscreen helps block harmful sun rays that can burn your skin.
quests.funFact: Sunscreen works best when you put it on again every two hours, or after swimming.

quests.instruction: When you put on sunscreen, which parts of your head are easy to forget, even though they can get burned?
quests.hint: They stick out on both sides of your head.
quests.explanation: Ears and the back of the neck often get missed, but they are in the sun just as much as your face.
quests.funFact: A hat with a wide brim shades your ears as well as your face.

quests.instruction: You practice a new song, then get a good night's sleep. Which part helps store what you learned?
quests.hint: It never fully switches off, even while you sleep.
quests.explanation: While you sleep, your brain sorts through the day and strengthens the memories of new things you learned.
quests.funFact: Kids aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night.

quests.instruction: After a hard day of play, rest and sleep give which parts time to repair and grow stronger?
quests.hint: They get tired after running and climbing.
quests.explanation: Exercise makes tiny tears in muscle fibers, and rest lets your body rebuild them stronger.
quests.funFact: Muscles do most of their growing while you rest, not while you play.

quests.instruction: Playing actively for about an hour a day helps keep which muscle in your chest strong?
quests.hint: It beats day and night.
quests.explanation: Active play makes your heart work harder, and that makes it stronger and better at pumping.
quests.funFact: Health experts suggest that children get about 60 minutes of active play each day.

quests.instruction: Sipping water after a meal helps rinse leftover food out of which part?
quests.hint: Food goes in through here.
quests.explanation: Water washes away food bits that stick around your teeth and gums.
quests.funFact: In many places, tap water has fluoride added, which helps protect teeth.

quests.instruction: It is a good idea to wait a little after a big meal before hard exercise, to give which part of your body time to start digesting?
quests.hint: It rumbles when you are hungry.
quests.explanation: After you eat, your tummy and the organs inside it get busy digesting. Gentle activity is fine, but waiting before a hard sprint feels better.
quests.funFact: Food's whole trip through your body, from the first bite to the end, can take a day or more.

quests.instruction: Milk, yogurt, and leafy greens contain calcium, which helps build strong what?
quests.hint: They are hard, and you grow most of them while you are young.
quests.explanation: Calcium is a mineral that helps make bones hard and strong.
quests.funFact: Bones are alive, and your body keeps rebuilding them throughout life.

quests.instruction: A car seat belt's lap strap should sit low across which part of your body?
quests.hint: It is below your waist, at the sides.
quests.explanation: A low lap belt rests on the strong hip bones, which can take the force in a sudden stop.
quests.funFact: Kids should ride in a car seat or booster until a seat belt fits them well.

quests.instruction: Which parts of your hands can get pinched in the gap on the hinge side of a door?
quests.hint: They are easy to leave in the wrong place.
quests.explanation: The gap by the hinge closes when the door shuts, so keep your fingers away from it.
quests.funFact: Some doors have finger guards, which are soft covers that fill the gap.

quests.instruction: When you ride a scooter, guards protect which joints if you fall on your outstretched hands?
quests.hint: They link your hands to your forearms.
quests.explanation: When you fall forward, your hands go out to catch you, and the wrists take a hard bump. Guards help soak it up.
quests.funFact: Wrist guards, a helmet, and knee and elbow pads work together as a team.

quests.instruction: After running and sweating, which parts of your body should you wash with soap so they do not get smelly?
quests.hint: They sit under your shoulders.
quests.explanation: Armpits get sweaty, and soap and water help keep them clean and fresh.
quests.funFact: Sweat itself has hardly any smell. The smell comes from tiny bacteria that feed on it.

quests.instruction: Which parts of your body are harmed by breathing smoky air, so it is best to stay away from smoke?
quests.hint: They fill with air when you breathe in.
quests.explanation: Smoke carries tiny particles and chemicals that irritate the lungs, which is why clean air matters.
quests.funFact: The tubes of your lungs have tiny hairs, called cilia, that sweep out dirt.

quests.instruction: A bike helmet is built to protect which part of your body, the part that controls everything you do?
quests.hint: It floats inside your head, cushioned by fluid.
quests.explanation: Your skull is strong, but a helmet's foam crushes in a crash and soaks up force that could hurt the brain.
quests.funFact: The foam in a helmet is meant to work once, so after a crash you need a new helmet.

quests.instruction: Tiny germs in your mouth turn leftover sugar into acid. Which parts of your body does that acid damage?
quests.hint: They are covered by a hard coating.
quests.explanation: Acid wears away enamel, which makes holes called cavities. Brushing removes the sugar and the germs.
quests.funFact: Saliva can repair tiny early damage to enamel, if you give your teeth a break between snacks.

quests.instruction: Sharing a cup or straw can pass germs from one person's what to another's?
quests.hint: It is the opening in your face used for eating and talking.
quests.explanation: A cup or straw carries a little spit, and germs along with it, from one mouth to the next. Use your own cup.
quests.funFact: Many colds spread through shared cups, hands, and tiny droplets.
